APX-000026.transcript:
Customer (Kevin Duncan): Can you explain how the equalization plan works out my monthly amount?
Agent (Zanele Radebe): Hi Kevin Duncan, Zanele Radebe here — let me pull that up.
Customer (Kevin Duncan): This is the third time this year my equalized amount has changed on me.
Agent (Zanele Radebe): Understood. Let me pull up the account and look at the charges before I say anything.
Agent (Zanele Radebe): Can you give me the account number from your bill, or the service address and the name on the account?
Customer (Kevin Duncan): Sure, it's the house on the account, and the bill's in my name.
Customer (Kevin Duncan): If the point of this plan is predictable payments, why does it keep moving?
Agent (Zanele Radebe): When did you first join the equalization plan?
Customer (Kevin Duncan): About two years ago, when we moved in.
Agent (Zanele Radebe): Has anything changed at home, like a new appliance or more people?
Customer (Kevin Duncan): We had a baby, so the heat's been on more.
Agent (Zanele Radebe): Would you rather stay on the plan or go back to regular billing?
Customer (Kevin Duncan): Stay on it, if it stops jumping around.
Agent (Zanele Radebe): Let me take a look. I've reviewed the equalization plan's 12-month usage average and the reconciliation adjustment that triggered the change.
Agent (Zanele Radebe): Thanks for holding — I've got the full picture now.
Agent (Zanele Radebe): The plan averages your last twelve months of usage and is reviewed at month six. If usage runs higher than the estimate, the difference is added.
Agent (Zanele Radebe): The plan recalculates twice a year against your rolling usage average, and this adjustment reflects higher usage than last year's estimate — I've set up an email alert so you'll get advance notice before the next recalculation instead of finding out on the bill.
Customer (Kevin Duncan): Will it change again without warning?
Agent (Zanele Radebe): The next review is in six months, and you'll get an email two weeks before it.
Agent (Zanele Radebe): To recap: the catch-up is spread over the rest of the plan year, and you'll get an email two weeks before the next review.
Customer (Kevin Duncan): Alright, thank you for looking into it.
Agent (Zanele Radebe): Thanks for bearing with me — you're all set.

Agent Zanele Radebe reviewed the equalization plan's 12-month usage average and the reconciliation adjustment that triggered the change. In the end, it was resolved on this interaction, and the customer rated it CSAT 4 (satisfied).

Customer (Amanda Thompson): Is the construction on my street part of the pipe replacement program, and how long will it last?
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): Hi Amanda Thompson, Nomsa Khumalo here — let me pull that up.
Customer (Amanda Thompson): Is my gas service going to be interrupted at any point during this work?
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): Thanks for letting us know. Let me check the project schedule for your street.
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): Can you give me the street address so I can match it to the project schedule?
Customer (Amanda Thompson): Our block, the crew's been there since Monday.
Customer (Amanda Thompson): Who do I actually call if the crew damages something on my property?
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): Do you need driveway access during the day?
Customer (Amanda Thompson): Yes, I leave for work at seven.
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): Did you see a door hanger or letter in the last few weeks?
Customer (Amanda Thompson): Nothing that I noticed.
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): Is anyone at home who relies on the gas during the day?
Customer (Amanda Thompson): My mother's home most days, and she needs the heat on.
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): Let me take a look. I've looked up the System Betterment Program schedule for that street segment and confirmed the notification timeline that was sent.
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): Okay, I've got it pulled up now.
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): This is the System Betterment Program, replacing older steel pipe on your street. A notice with the timeline and a site contact should have gone out two weeks ahead.
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): This is the pre-1975 pipe replacement work under our System Betterment Program — a notice with the timeline and a site contact number should have gone out two weeks ahead, I've resent it to your address and confirmed there's no planned service interruption.
Customer (Amanda Thompson): How long will the street be dug up?
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): About two weeks on your block, with the road restored after.
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): To recap: two weeks on your block, a door knock before any interruption, and the notice with the site contact is in your email.
Customer (Amanda Thompson): Alright, thank you for looking into it.
Agent (Nomsa Khumalo): Thanks for bearing with me — you're all set.

APX-000041.transcript:
Customer (Amanda Baker): Someone told me I'm being moved to a different rate class because of the August rate change. Is that true?
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Hi Amanda Baker, Sipho van der Merwe here — let me pull that up.
Customer (Amanda Baker): I've been on the same rate for years, why is this changing now?
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Happy to explain it. Let me pull up your usage first.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Can you give me the account number from your bill, or the service address and the name on the account?
Customer (Amanda Baker): Yes, same address as always, and the account's under my name.
Customer (Amanda Baker): Is this the Phase 2 thing the AUC approved, or did I do something wrong on my account?
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Is this a home, a farm, or a business account?
Customer (Amanda Baker): It's our home. We're not a business.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Did you get the letter by mail or by email?
Customer (Amanda Baker): By mail, a couple of weeks ago.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Do you have any irrigation or shop meters on the same account?
Customer (Amanda Baker): No, just the house.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Let me take a look. I've pulled up the account, confirmed the Rate 1/Rate 2 threshold under the August 1 Phase 2 restructuring, and walked through what changed on this specific account.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Thanks for holding — I've got the full picture now.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Since August 1, Rate 1 covers accounts using under 4,000 GJ a year and Rate 2 covers larger users. The AUC approved it as Phase 2 of the rate restructuring.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Your annual usage is well under that, so you stay on Rate 1. What changed is how the distribution charge is shown on the bill.
Customer (Amanda Baker): Okay. What's the actual next step here?
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Give me one more moment while I confirm the details.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): You're on Rate 1 since your annual usage is under 4,000 GJ, so the main change is the way the distribution charge is broken out on the bill — your total shouldn't move much. I've sent the AUC decision summary to your email so you have it on file.
Customer (Amanda Baker): So my total won't go up much?
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): It shouldn't. Most of this month's jump is colder weather, not the rate change.
Customer (Amanda Baker): Can I get that in writing?
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): The AUC summary and your usage figure are in your email now.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): To recap: you're staying on Rate 1, the change is mostly how the bill is laid out, and the summary is in your email.
Customer (Amanda Baker): Alright, thank you for looking into it.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Thanks for bearing with me — you're all set.
APX-000041.narrative_summary: Amanda Baker, an Apex Utilities customer, contacted support on a rate-class change case. Agent Sipho van der Merwe pulled up the account, confirmed the Rate 1/Rate 2 threshold under the August 1 Phase 2 restructuring, and walked through what changed on this specific account. In the end, it was resolved on this interaction, and the customer rated it CSAT 5 (very satisfied).

APX-000042.transcript:
Customer (Kevin Young): I smell gas in my basement and I don't know what to do.
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): Hi Kevin Young, Lerato Ndlovu here — let me pull that up.
Customer (Kevin Young): How long until someone actually gets here?
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): You did the right thing calling. Let's get you safe first.
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): Are you and everyone else out of the house now? What's the address?
Customer (Kevin Young): Yes, we're all out. The address is on the account.
Customer (Kevin Young): Is it safe for me to stay in the house right now?
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): Can you still smell it from where you're standing?
Customer (Kevin Young): A little, near the side of the house.
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): Is anyone in the house who couldn't get out?
Customer (Kevin Young): No, everyone's out, the dog too.
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): Is there a phone number the technician can reach you on?
Customer (Kevin Young): This one. I'll keep it on me.
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): Let me take a look. I've dispatched an emergency field technician immediately and stayed on the line with safety instructions.
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): Alright, I can see exactly what's going on here.
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): A technician is being sent now. Gas odour calls go straight to the front of the queue.
Customer (Kevin Young): Okay. What's the actual next step here?
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): Give me one more moment while I confirm the details.
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): A technician is on the way and should be there within 30 minutes — in the meantime, don't use any switches or open flames, and I'll call you back the moment they're on site.
Customer (Kevin Young): What will they do when they get here?
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): Check the house and meter for leaks and make it safe. They won't leave until it is.
Customer (Kevin Young): Should we call the fire department?
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): If the smell gets stronger or you hear a loud hiss, yes, call 911 as well.
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): To recap: the technician is on the way, stay outside, and don't use switches or flames until they've checked it.
Customer (Kevin Young): Alright, thank you for looking into it.
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): Thanks for bearing with me — you're all set.

Agent Lerato Ndlovu dispatched an emergency field technician immediately and stayed on the line with safety instructions. Customer (Mark Ross): I got a letter about a 'Rate 1' and 'Rate 2' change and I have no idea what it means for my bill.
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Hi Mark Ross, Naledi Nkosi here — let me pull that up.
Customer (Mark Ross): Is this the Phase 2 thing the AUC approved, or did I do something wrong on my account?
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Good question, a lot of customers are asking about this one. Let me check your account.
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Can you give me the account number from your bill, or the service address and the name on the account?
Customer (Mark Ross): Yes, same address as always, and the account's under my name.
Customer (Mark Ross): I've been on the same rate for years, why is this changing now?
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Is this a home, a farm, or a business account?
Customer (Mark Ross): It's our home. We're not a business.
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Roughly how much gas do you use in a year, or should I look it up?
Customer (Mark Ross): No idea. Can you look it up?
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Did you get the letter by mail or by email?

Customer (Mark Ross): Okay. What's the actual next step here?
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Give me one more moment while I confirm the details.
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): You're on Rate 1 since your annual usage is under 4,000 GJ, so the main change is the way the distribution charge is broken out on the bill — your total shouldn't move much. I've sent the AUC decision summary to your email so you have it on file.
Customer (Mark Ross): So my total won't go up much?
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): It shouldn't. Most of this month's jump is colder weather, not the rate change.
Customer (Mark Ross): Can I get that in writing?
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): The AUC summary and your usage figure are in your email now.
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): To recap: you're staying on Rate 1, the change is mostly how the bill is laid out, and the summary is in your email.
Customer (Mark Ross): Alright, thank you for looking into it.
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Thanks for bearing with me — you're all set.

Customer (David Anderson): I need to dispute this bill. The fees on it don't make sense.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Hi David Anderson, Sipho van der Merwe here — let me pull that up.
Customer (David Anderson): Can you actually break down where every line item on this bill comes from?
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Thanks for bearing with us on this. Let me go through the bill with you properly.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Can you give me the account number from your bill, or the service address and the name on the account?
Customer (David Anderson): Yes, same address as always, and the account's under my name.
Customer (David Anderson): This isn't the first time — I feel like I'm being charged fees just for having an account.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Which line items are you disputing?
Customer (David Anderson): The distribution charge and the fixed charge. They're bigger than the gas.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Is the property occupied at the moment?
Customer (David Anderson): It's vacant while we sell it, so the gas is barely on.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Let me take a look. I've reviewed the itemized charges line by line against metered usage and the current distribution rate schedule.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Okay, I've got it pulled up now.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): The distribution charge and the fixed daily charge are set by the AUC for your rate class, so they apply even when the meter reads zero.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): The distribution and fixed charges you're seeing are billed under the AUC-approved rate schedule regardless of how much gas you actually use that month — I can explain the structure, but I don't have the authority to waive a regulated charge.
Customer (David Anderson): So there's nothing you can do?
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): I can't waive a regulated charge. I can send the dispute to a billing specialist so every line is checked, not just explained.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): To recap: the regulated charges stand, a billing specialist is checking each line, and you'll hear back within five business days.
Customer (David Anderson): Alright, thank you for looking into it.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Thanks for bearing with me — you're all set.

APX-000318.transcript:
Customer (James Stewart): I got a letter about a 'Rate 1' and 'Rate 2' change and I have no idea what it means for my bill.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): Hi James Stewart, Vusi Jacobs here — let me pull that up.
Customer (James Stewart): I've been on the same rate for years, why is this changing now?
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): Happy to explain it. Let me pull up your usage first.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): Can you give me the account number from your bill, or the service address and the name on the account?
Customer (James Stewart): Yes, same address as always, and the account's under my name.
Customer (James Stewart): Is this the Phase 2 thing the AUC approved, or did I do something wrong on my account?
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): Is this a home, a farm, or a business account?
Customer (James Stewart): It's our home. We're not a business.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): Did you get the letter by mail or by email?
Customer (James Stewart): By mail, a couple of weeks ago.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): Do you have any irrigation or shop meters on the same account?
Customer (James Stewart): No, just the house.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): Let me take a look. I've pulled up the account, confirmed the Rate 1/Rate 2 threshold under the August 1 Phase 2 restructuring, and walked through what changed on this specific account.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): Thanks for holding — I've got the full picture now.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): Since August 1, Rate 1 covers accounts using under 4,000 GJ a year and Rate 2 covers larger users. The AUC approved it as Phase 2 of the rate restructuring.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): Your annual usage is well under that, so you stay on Rate 1. What changed is how the distribution charge is shown on the bill.
Customer (James Stewart): Okay. What's the actual next step here?
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): Give me one more moment while I confirm the details.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): Your usage puts you right at the edge of the new Rate 2 threshold, so this bill reflects the higher rate class — I don't have authority to move you back to Rate 1 manually, that's set by your metered usage under the AUC-approved structure.
Customer (James Stewart): Can't you just put me back on Rate 1?
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): Not manually. The class follows your metered usage under the approved structure.
Customer (James Stewart): What happens if my usage drops next year?
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): The class is reviewed against your annual usage, so it would move back if you fall under the threshold. I've noted that on the account.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): To recap: your usage puts you in Rate 2 for now, the class is reviewed against annual usage, and the details are in your email.
Customer (James Stewart): Alright, thank you for looking into it.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): Thanks for bearing with me — you're all set.

APX-000538.transcript:
Customer (Susan Scott): The furnace makes a soft whoosh when it comes on. Should I be worried?
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Hi Susan Scott, Sipho van der Merwe here — let me pull that up.
Customer (Susan Scott): Is this something I should be worried about, or is it normal?
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Happy to help with that.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Before I go into the account, can you confirm the service address and the account holder's name?
Customer (Susan Scott): Yes, same address as always, and the account's under my name.
Customer (Susan Scott): Should I have someone look at it, or is it fine to keep using?
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Do you smell gas at all right now?
Customer (Susan Scott): No, nothing like that.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): How old is the furnace?
Customer (Susan Scott): About fifteen years.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): When was it last serviced by a licensed technician?
Customer (Susan Scott): A couple of years ago, I think.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Let me take a look. I've walked through the standard non-emergency safety guidance and checked for any signs that needed a field visit.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Alright, I can see exactly what's going on here.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): A few clicks or a soft whoosh before the burner lights is the igniter and the gas catching. That's normal on most furnaces.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Apex looks after the meter and the line to your house. The furnace itself is serviced by a licensed heating contractor.
Customer (Susan Scott): Okay. What's the actual next step here?
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Give me one more moment while I confirm the details.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): What you're describing is the normal ignition sequence, so there's nothing to worry about. If the sound changes, or you ever smell gas, call us straight away.
Customer (Susan Scott): So I don't need anything from Apex?
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Not for this. A yearly service by a licensed technician is still a good idea at fifteen years.
Customer (Susan Scott): And if I ever do smell gas?
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Leave the house and call our 24-hour emergency line from outside.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): To recap: the ignition sound is normal, a yearly service is worth booking, and the emergency line is there if you ever smell gas.
Customer (Susan Scott): Alright, thank you for looking into it.
Agent (Sipho van der Merwe): Thanks for bearing with me — you're all set.

Customer (David Bell): Our furnace takes a few seconds to light after the fan starts. Is that a problem?
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Hi David Bell, Naledi Nkosi here — let me pull that up.
Customer (David Bell): Should I have someone look at it, or is it fine to keep using?

Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Do you smell gas at all right now?

Agent (Naledi Nkosi): How old is the furnace?

Agent (Naledi Nkosi): What you're describing is the normal ignition sequence, so there's nothing to worry about. If the sound changes, or you ever smell gas, call us straight away.

Agent (Naledi Nkosi): To recap: the ignition sound is normal, a yearly service is worth booking, and the emergency line is there if you ever smell gas.
Customer (David Bell): Alright, thank you for looking into it.
Agent (Naledi Nkosi): Thanks for bearing with me — you're all set.

Customer (Sarah Duncan): I'm following up again — I signed up for budget billing so my payments would be predictable, and now I've got a CA$600 catch-up bill.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): Hi Sarah Duncan, Vusi Jacobs here — let me pull that up.
Customer (Sarah Duncan): I already explained this on my last contact.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): I'm sorry about that — let me look at what happened last time and pick up from there.
Customer (Sarah Duncan): This is the third time this year my equalized amount has changed on me.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): Understood. Let me pull up the account and look at the charges before I say anything.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): Before I go into the account, can you confirm the service address and the account holder's name?
Customer (Sarah Duncan): Yes, same address as always, and the account's under my name.
Customer (Sarah Duncan): If the point of this plan is predictable payments, why does it keep moving?
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): When did you first join the equalization plan?
Customer (Sarah Duncan): About two years ago, when we moved in.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): Has anything changed at home, like a new appliance or more people?
Customer (Sarah Duncan): We had a baby, so the heat's been on more.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): Would you rather stay on the plan or go back to regular billing?
Customer (Sarah Duncan): Stay on it, if it stops jumping around.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): Let me take a look. I've reviewed the equalization plan's 12-month usage average and the reconciliation adjustment that triggered the change.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): Thanks for holding — I've got the full picture now.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): The plan averages your last twelve months of usage and is reviewed at month six. If usage runs higher than the estimate, the difference is added.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): The equalization amount is recalculated from your usage history under the plan terms, and I can't reverse an adjustment that's already been applied — what I can do is flag your file so the next change comes with a heads-up call before it hits your bill.
Customer (Sarah Duncan): So the CA$600 is still due?
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): The adjustment has been applied and I can't reverse it. I can split it over two payments instead of one.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): To recap: the adjustment stands, it can be split over two payments, and your file is flagged for a call before the next change.
Customer (Sarah Duncan): That's not really the answer I was hoping for, but okay.
Agent (Vusi Jacobs): I've logged everything here so if this comes up again, the next agent has the full picture.

Customer (Ryan Anderson): I'm following up again — I need to close my account at the old address and set up payments for the new one.

Customer (Karen Cameron): I'm following up again — this bill says 'estimated read' again. Can someone come and read my meter?
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): Hi Karen Cameron, Lerato Ndlovu here — let me pull that up.
Customer (Karen Cameron): I already explained this on my last contact.
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): I'm sorry about that — let me look at what happened last time and pick up from there.
Customer (Karen Cameron): If the estimate is wrong, how does the correction actually happen on a future bill?
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): Thanks for bearing with us on this. Let me go through the bill with you properly.
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): Before I go into the account, can you confirm the service address and the account holder's name?
Customer (Karen Cameron): Yes, same address as always, and the account's under my name.
Customer (Karen Cameron): Is there a way I can submit my own meter reading instead of waiting?
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): Do you have a reading from the meter today?
Customer (Karen Cameron): I took a photo this morning. It's much lower than the bill.
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): How many estimated bills have you had in a row?
Customer (Karen Cameron): Three, I think.
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): Let me take a look. I've checked the meter-read schedule for the account and confirmed whether a self-read or field read was available.
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): Okay, I've got it pulled up now.
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): When our reader can't reach the meter, the bill is estimated from your past usage for the same months.
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): Your meter is on the standard bi-monthly read cycle, so this cycle is estimated by design — I've noted your account for a field read next cycle, but I can't move today's estimate to an actual reading.
Customer (Karen Cameron): So this month's estimate just stands?
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): For this cycle, yes. It corrects itself once there's an actual read.
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): To recap: this estimate stands for now, a field read is booked for next cycle, and any difference is corrected on that bill.
Customer (Karen Cameron): Alright, thank you for looking into it.
Agent (Lerato Ndlovu): Thanks for bearing with me — you're all set.
